rationale: B wins because it gives the founder more usable reporting paths without pretending one launch can carry the whole travel-tech universe. A's best line, "The AI travel planner that books nothing," is good, but it props itself up with "the prevailing belief, loudly marketed across the industry" without supplied evidence. B's "The math behind Going's claim that paid members save $550 a flight" and its referral-revenue/roadmap questions are exactly the kind of proof-first angles that survive a reporter's second email.
gaps_in_A: "the prevailing belief, loudly marketed across the industry" is imported context, not in the update; the no-booking angle is strong enough without decorating it as an industrywide revolt.
"the deal that lands in your inbox" invents the delivery channel. The update says the app finds a fare alert, not that this specific launch is email-led.
The set misses a clean data angle around "$550 per booked flight" as its own story; it only treats the number as support for the paywall angle.
"pick one angle ... the contrarian 'books nothing' framing is the most differentiated" is too confident before the company explains why it stops at link-out.
gaps_in_B: "gates its first AI feature to Premium" invents "first." The update only says this planner is Premium-only.
"newsletter-born audiences" and "free list" import company history not supplied in the update. Formerly Scott's Cheap Flights is a fact; newsletter-born is not in the packet.
"to convert 2 million free deal-hunters" states motive as fact. Paywall implies a conversion question, not a proven strategy.
"the company's own phrasing says 'yet'" over-attributes the prompt wording to the company. Useful question, sloppy sourcing.
